big: A REIT yields 7% and the client says, 'That is better than my deposit.' But REIT units trade on an exchange and can fall sharply. A yield is not a promise, and it is not a deposit rate.

lines: Price risk: units can fall in weak markets or when rates rise. Interest rate risk: higher rates raise borrowing costs and make deposits more attractive. Asset risk: lower occupancy, tenant exits or falling traffic cut income. Leverage risk: borrowing is capped at 49% of asset value. And some units trade thinly.

intro: Rules as in the lesson; confirm current SEBI rules before advising.

q: How can higher interest rates hurt units?
opts: Always lift every unit price up
Remove all the risk from units
Fix the payout for many years
why: They do not always lift prices. The details here point elsewhere.
Costs rise and alternatives look better. That matches the case described.
Risk is not removed. That does not match this case.
Payouts are not fixed. It does not fit the facts given.

q: What is the leverage cap in the lesson?

opts: A change in the unit's logo
A new design for the brochure
A longer lunch at the office
why: Both cut the income that units pay out.
A logo does not change the income paid.
A brochure does not change the income.
Lunch breaks do not change the income.

q: Why compare a yield with a deposit rate carefully?
opts: Both are exactly the same product
Both are insured by the law
Units can fall; payouts can change

pts: Price, interest rate, asset, leverage and liquidity risks.
Leverage is capped at 49% of asset value.
A yield is not a promise or a deposit rate.
